subject: ela
description: Students explain how an author develops the point of view of the narrator or speaker in a literary text. They identify whether a narrator speaks in first person (I, we, me) or third person (he, she, they), and within third person distinguish limited from omniscient narration. They explain how the chosen point of view shapes what the reader knows, what is hidden, and how the reader feels about characters and events. They trace the specific words, pronouns, thoughts, and details an author uses to build and reveal a narrator's or speaker's perspective, including the perspective of a poem's speaker. Every item embeds the full excerpt or short passage it depends on, so the student needs nothing external.
subSkills: Identify the narrator's point of view from pronouns and access to thought (first person vs. third person; within third person, limited vs. omniscient)
Determine the perspective, attitude, or feelings of the narrator or speaker toward characters, events, or subjects in the text
Explain how the chosen point of view controls what the reader can and cannot know (whose thoughts are revealed, what information is withheld)
Cite the specific words, pronouns, thoughts, and details the author uses to develop and reveal the point of view
Analyze how the point of view shapes the reader's understanding of and feelings toward characters and events
Identify and interpret the perspective of a speaker in a poem, distinguishing the speaker from the poet

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the narrator's point of view
problemArchetypes.example: Read the excerpt: 'I pressed my face to the cold window and counted the cars below, wishing my brother would finally come home.' From whose point of view is this passage told? Answer: First person, because the narrator uses 'I' and 'my' and shares only his or her own thoughts and feelings.

problemArchetypes.name: Limited vs. omniscient third person
problemArchetypes.example: Read the excerpt: 'Dana smiled at the gift, but inside she dreaded the long visit ahead. Across the room, her aunt felt the same secret worry, though neither of them said a word.' Is this narrator third person limited or third person omniscient? Answer: Omniscient, because the narrator reveals the private thoughts of more than one character.

problemArchetypes.name: Determine the narrator's or speaker's attitude
problemArchetypes.example: Read the excerpt: 'My cousin called it the trip of a lifetime. Six hours in a hot car listening to him brag about his trophies. Some lifetime.' What is the narrator's attitude toward the trip? Answer: Sarcastic and unimpressed; the narrator mocks the idea that the trip was special, shown by 'Some lifetime.'

problemArchetypes.name: Explain what the point of view lets the reader know or hides
problemArchetypes.example: Read the excerpt: 'Sam watched the new student eat lunch alone and decided she must be unfriendly. He did not know she had moved three times that year.' How does the point of view shape what the reader knows? Answer: The narrator stays close to Sam's limited view, so the reader first shares his mistaken judgment, then learns the truth he cannot see, which builds sympathy for the new student.

problemArchetypes.name: Cite the details that develop the point of view
problemArchetypes.example: Read the excerpt: 'We never locked our doors back then. We knew every face on the street, and every face knew ours.' Which words show that the narrator is part of the community being described, and how does that build the point of view? Answer: The repeated 'we' and 'our' show the narrator speaks as an insider remembering a shared past, giving the passage a warm, nostalgic perspective.

problemArchetypes.name: Interpret the speaker's perspective in a poem
problemArchetypes.example: Read the poem: 'They handed me the smallest oar / and told me I would only row, / but watch the water learn my name / the day I choose where we will go.' What is the speaker's perspective on being given a small role? Answer: The speaker feels underestimated but determined; the lines suggest confidence that the speaker will one day lead, shown by 'where we will go.'

Easy.description: A short excerpt of roughly 2 to 4 sentences (about 20 to 45 words) embedded in the item, written in a clearly marked point of view with obvious pronoun signals. The task is identify-level: name the point of view (first person or third person) or state the narrator's plainly stated feeling. The answer is supported by surface pronouns and direct statements, with little inference required.
constraints: Stimulus is a 2 to 4 sentence excerpt included in the prompt, simple vocabulary and sentence structure
Point of view is signaled clearly by pronouns (I/we vs. he/she/they)
Identify-level task: name the point of view or the narrator's stated attitude
Answer is supported by explicit text; minimal inference

Medium.description: A passage of roughly 4 to 7 sentences (about 50 to 90 words) embedded in the item, with a more developed narrator or speaker. The task is analyze-level: distinguish third person limited from omniscient, determine an attitude that is implied rather than stated, or explain how the point of view shapes what the reader knows about one or two characters. The student must connect specific words or details to the perspective they create.
constraints: Stimulus is a 4 to 7 sentence passage or a short poem stanza included in the prompt, grade-level vocabulary
Tests limited vs. omniscient, implied attitude, or how point of view controls reader knowledge
Analyze-level task: cite words or details and explain the perspective they build
Requires moderate inference; distractors are plausible partial readings

Hard.description: A richer passage of roughly 7 to 12 sentences (about 90 to 150 words) or a full short poem embedded in the item, with a subtle or unreliable narrator, an ironic gap between what the narrator believes and what the reader infers, or a perspective that shifts or contrasts with another character's. The task is evaluate-level: explain how the author develops the point of view across the passage, judge how it shapes the reader's feelings, or analyze the effect of a gap between the narrator's view and reality. Requires sustained inference and synthesis of several details.
constraints: Stimulus is a 7 to 12 sentence passage or a complete short poem included in the prompt, with subtlety or irony
Contains an unreliable, biased, or contrasting perspective, or a gap between narrator belief and reader inference
Evaluate-level task: explain how the author develops point of view and its effect on the reader, citing multiple details
Requires sustained inference and synthesis across the whole passage

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the narrator or speaker with the author, assuming the views expressed are the writer's own
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims the passage shows what the author believes or feels, rather than the perspective of the narrator or speaker created within the text

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student labels any third person narrator as omniscient, not checking whether more than one character's thoughts are actually revealed
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls a passage omniscient even though the narrator reports only one character's inner thoughts, which makes it third person limited

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student decides point of view by who the story is about rather than who is telling it and which pronouns are used
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls a first person account 'third person' because it describes other characters, ignoring the 'I' and 'my' that mark the narrator

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student takes the narrator's stated judgment at face value and misses irony, bias, or an unreliable perspective
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports the narrator's biased or mistaken opinion as the truth of the story instead of recognizing the gap the author builds between the narrator's view and reality

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student names the point of view but cannot connect it to its effect, treating point of view as a label with no consequence for meaning
commonMisconceptions.distractor: States the correct point of view yet selects an explanation that does not link it to what the reader knows, feels, or cannot see

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student mistakes the narrator's neutral or descriptive tone for a strong attitude, or reads emotion into a perspective that the text does not support
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Assigns an exaggerated feeling such as anger or joy to the narrator when the embedded words and details support a calm, neutral, or different attitude
